To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PRL alters the mammary epithelial hierarchy, increasing progenitors and facilitating ovarian steroid action.

PRL can alter the mammary epithelial hierarchy, even without ovarian hormones, by increasing stem cells and progenitors and that PRL can also alter the actions of ovarian hormones on the mammary epithelium.
PRL can alter the mammary epithelial hierarchy, increase progenitors, and facilitate steroid actions, which may underly its role in the pathogenesis of breast cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that regulate the development of the mammary gland.

understanding how prolactin (a hormone that is produced by the pituitary gland) and ovarian steroids (hormones that are produced by the ovary) interact to control the normal development and function of the mammary gland and how these hormones may contribute to the development of breast tumors.
how hormones drive mammary development, and how this process is altered by the environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

PRL can act alone and with ovarian steroids to increase the mammary epithelial hierarchy and alter transcriptional networks, which may contribute to the increased risk for ERα+ breast cancer associated with PRL exposure.
PRL can influence the epithelial stem/progenitor hierarchy, even in the absence of ovarian steroids, and may facilitate some ovarian steroid actions, but also can oppose them.
PRL can alter the hierarchy of stem/progenitors, even without ovarian steroid exposure, and with steroids can further increase the activity of these populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prolactin (a hormone produced by the pituitary gland) can influence the development of the mammary gland and can influence the risk of breast cancer.
PRL is a hormone that can drive the mammary gland to become more stem cell-like and that can oppose the action of ovarian steroids on mammary stem cells.

prolactin (a hormone that is produced by the pituitary gland and secreted into the blood) can alter the hierarchy of mammary cells (i.e., the order of cells that are formed in the breast) and increase the number of cells that have the ability to become a new breast.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PRL can drive mammary development, and in particular stem cell activity, and it can modulate the effects of estrogen and progesterone.
PRL can alter the mammary epithelial hierarchy and increase the activity of progenitors, even without ovarian steroid hormones.
PRL is a potent modulator of the epithelial hierarchy in the mammary gland.
